titleStmt.title: To Harriet Shaw Weaver. Friday, 6 October 1922
titleStmt.author: James Joyce

seriesStmt.p: Machine readable texts of the unpublished correspondence of James Joyce

projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p: Dear Miss Weaver: I shall not start till Tuesday so if Mr Rodker is here on Monday he can see me. I shall stop a night and half a day in Dijon. Dr Borsch’s opinion was more favourable yesterday. He will not correct the lens till I come back but he says he thinks the nebula is not organised. Anyhow I was able to read very small print with both eyes open—of course, in a good light my right eye doing the work which however the left did not impede. Will you please add Mr Schiff’s name to group A? It seems that the Evening Standard sent to Dublin marked with red pencil did not arrive owing to postal strike. I shall be much obliged if you will send a copy to the following in A: John Joyce Mrs Murray Michael Healy. This is not vainglorious on my part but a policy or part of one.

div.note: In the following week, JJ would depart for Nice with his family where he would stay until mid-November 1922.

JJ planned to stop in Dijon on his way to Nice to meet with printer Maurice Darantiere. “At Dijon I spoke to Mr Darantiere who thinks that the corrections of plates ought to be begun at once so whenever a third edition is called for the book can appear letter perfect,” JJ wrote to Weaver in a letter on 17 October 1922 from Nice (LI 188).

Dr Borsch, JJ’s ophthalmologist, returned to Paris at the beginning of October and approved JJ’s winter holiday in Nice. Borsch advised JJ to undergo a complete dental extraction in Nice to prepare for a sphincterectomy upon his return to Paris. JJ would postpone the dental and optical surgeries until early 1923 (JJ 536-7; 543).
In examining JJ’s nebula, Dr Borsch concluded that JJ was unlikely to develop glaucoma and that his condition was less severe than the London ophthalmologists had supposed (JJ 537).

The list of people who were to receive a copy of the Egoist Press edition of Ulysses, with the heading “Group A”, is kept at the British Library (BL 57356-14; JJA 12: 188). “Mr Sydney Schiff” is added as the last item.
Possibly the review “A Monstrous Book” in the London Evening Standard from which Sisley Huddleston later quoted extensively in Paris Salons, Cafés, Studios (1928, pp. 208-20).

The Dublin Postal Strike of 1922 occurred in September 1922, after workers became frustrated with the Irish Free State Government’s attitude. The strike was a reaction to the government’s attempt to cut ‘cost of living’ bonuses.
